The historic data figures on case load tallies is from way too long ago to have ANY relevance present day.

Far too many variables in the equation have long since changed since then (2009). Historic data in any database in Corporate America is only valuable for roughly 3 years - max of 5 years, if precious little changed in its configuration, data field values and their defining criteria rules. 11-year-old data is an absolute joke that would only serve to mislead people and drive them to make poor decisions if that's their source of data used in decision making.

A much better approach for comparison sake would be to look at year-over-year numbers for the past several years. Much more recent years evaluating variations in tallies (between 2020 vs. 2019 vs. 2018) would be the only stats where the data stats would be even close to retaining its data consistency and data integrity for a span of time.

You could use current 2020 year stats and compare to 2019 and 2018 probably, but it's only actually "clean" data if nothing in the database configuration or any of the data fields (or combination/grouped) data fields have been changed that entire time over the 3-year period. Even if the data field names themselves haven't changed, the data input that populates those data fields (originating sources that push data figures into assigned data fields) could also have changed or the data field may suddenly be altered to containing a combination of numbers from multiple sources - things like that.

A typical PACER user would probably not have any inkling about the guts or back-end of how the database is configured or what the data rules/parameters are that are set for each data field. They may not even know an updated software release was pushed into the system overnight unless it broke something they were trying to work on.

All I'm getting at is there are a ton of factors that can impact the viability and 'clean'-ness of data. The older it is, the more tainted and less valuable it becomes. Companies using software-as-a-service will typically get a 3-5 year contract, after which they may change software providers and gut their whole system to migrate over to a different platform/vendor. Migrations are notorious for blowing up all kinds of data and once the data is corrupted, there's really no un-fucking it.

There may not even BE a data field for "indictments" specifically to even sort the data by in Pacer. Or if there is a data field called "Indictments" it may be user-access limited to a certain admin-rights level or managerial pay grade.
